input: A new workspace has no anki-language.config.json. User provides a lesson in French.
expected: Before analyzing the lesson, asks for target language.
Before analyzing the lesson, asks for base language.
Does not infer French as the target solely from the source.
Does not default the base language to English or any other language.
Persists the answered pair for later runs.

input: Workspace configuration says target Japanese and base Portuguese.
expected: Uses Japanese as the target language.
Uses Portuguese for explanations, translations, cues, and production prompts.
Does not introduce English unless the source itself requires it.

input: Target-language text contains a useful unfamiliar chunk.
expected: Uses a base-language semantic cue when a production card is valuable.
Does not use a blind cloze.
May create more than one card only for distinct skills.

input: Material contains an item the learner already knows well.
expected: May create zero cards.
Does not create cards merely to fill every deck type.

input: User supplies native target-language audio for a useful sentence plus its transcript.
expected: Listening puts original audio on the front.
Transcript and configured base-language meaning are on the back.
A production sibling is created only if independently valuable.

input: Learner confuses two target-language sounds and provides separate native recordings.
expected: Uses Pronunciation & Sounds.
Audio is on the front.
Written answer is not shown on the front.

input: Text-only material introduces a concrete noun.
expected: May use a useful permitted image.
Does not add decorative images to unrelated abstract items.
Records media provenance when known.

input: One useful target-language sentence is supplied. Only written recognition is actually difficult for the learner.
expected: Creates only the useful Reading card.
Does not create Listening, Production, or Pronunciation siblings merely because those templates exist.

input: A proposed Production card is: I ___ staying home. The intended target is the equivalent of 'ended up'.
expected: Rejects the unconstrained blank as ambiguous.
Adds a semantic/function cue in the configured base language or uses a direct guided-production prompt.
Does not make the learner guess the author's intended answer.

input: A target-language expression is useful for comprehension but not yet important for active production.
expected: Creates a recognition card only.
Does not create an automatic base-to-target reverse card.

input: Cards from several target languages and skills will be reviewed together.
expected: Every card front identifies the configured target language and trained skill.
The context label does not reveal the answer.

input: The useful knowledge is a fixed target-language collocation whose individual words are already known.
expected: Prioritizes the collocation/chunk as the retrieval target.
Does not create redundant isolated-word cards solely because the words appear in the phrase.

input: A native audio sentence contains a useful chunk. The learner has difficulty understanding the sentence by ear and also wants to actively use the chunk in speech.
expected: May create a Listening card from the audio.
May create a separate Production card from the same source sentence because it trains a different retrieval operation.
Does not treat reuse of the same source as duplication when the skills are genuinely distinct.
Creates no additional Reading or Pronunciation card unless those skills have independent learning value.

input: A sentence already has a useful Reading card. Listening, Production, and Pronunciation versions would add little or no new learning value.
expected: Keeps the useful Reading card.
Rejects low-value sibling cards even though the same source could technically be reused.
Prioritizes memory efficiency per review minute over extracting the maximum number of cards.

input: A useful target-language sentence should train Listening but the material has text only.
expected: Creates a Listening card only if Listening is worthwhile.
Adds an audio_request for the target sentence instead of inventing a fake audio path.
Uses automatic TTS only after user/native audio is unavailable.
Requires functional audio validation before APKG or live delivery.

input: A concrete noun would be learned faster from a clear image and no image was supplied.
expected: May create an image_request with a precise search query.
Prefers licensed/open media and records provenance.
Does not attach the image unless the downloaded file decodes successfully.

input: An abstract connector such as 'however/nevertheless' already has a clear production cue.
expected: Does not search for an image merely because automatic image search exists.
Prioritizes a concise text/production card.

input: A generated/downloaded audio or image file is corrupt or fails decoding.
expected: Rejects the file before APKG packaging or AnkiConnect addNotes.
Blocks delivery when the media is required.
Skips and records the issue when the media is optional.
Never claims that the media was successfully delivered.

input: User asks for direct Anki delivery through AnkiConnect with audio and image.
expected: Validates local media before upload.
Preflights notes.
After creation, verifies the note field references the uploaded filename.
Retrieves media from Anki and compares it against the local SHA-256 before reporting success.

input: A learner confuses two target-language sounds. Two candidate audio sets exist: one uses the same speaker/recording conditions for both words; the other uses visibly different speakers and volume levels.
expected: Prefers the matched-speaker/matched-condition pair when quality is otherwise acceptable.
Uses the audio contrast to test the target sound rather than incidental speaker/microphone cues.
Does not block a useful minimal-pair card if only different-speaker recordings are available.

input: The learner has already demonstrated reliable automatic grapheme-to-sound mapping on representative examples; a new easy word follows the same pattern.
expected: Does not create another spelling/spelling-sound card merely because that card type exists.
Creates one only if the new item has genuinely difficult or exceptional orthography/sound mapping.
Does not use a fixed universal 100–300 word cutoff.

input: A comprehension/usage card asks the learner to demonstrate a valid context for a target word. The stored example differs from the learner's natural but correct example.
expected: Treats the learner's natural semantically correct usage as success.
Does not require verbatim reproduction of the stored example when exact wording is not the target.
Still requires a clear prompt and rejects usages that do not demonstrate the intended meaning/form.

input: An intermediate learner can easily understand a concise target-language definition of a new word; a longer monolingual definition would introduce several unknown terms.
expected: May use the concise target-language definition.
Rejects the harder definition that creates extra learning targets.
May still use the configured base language when it is clearer/faster; does not enforce monolinguality.

input: While reading a chapter, the learner encounters eight unfamiliar words. Some recur in useful context, some are trivial/rare, and some are already inferable.
expected: Treats all eight as candidates rather than automatically creating eight cards.
Preserves sentence/source context when practical.
Selects cards only after applying usefulness, distinctness, context, and future review-cost criteria.
May batch the decision after the passage/chapter to avoid interrupting reading.

input: A simple production card is already clear, but the workflow could spend extra time finding decorative images, multiple pronunciations, and extensive styling.
expected: Keeps the simpler card when the extra customization would not materially improve retrieval.
Treats card-creation time as part of the cost function.
Uses automation to reduce friction rather than justify unnecessary decoration.

input: A production card tests one conjugated form. A one-sentence rule would prevent a likely confusion, while a full conjugation table and long AI grammar breakdown are also available.
expected: Adds the short rule or contrast on the back.
Does not paste the full paradigm or long explanation by default.
Keeps the front focused on the retrieval target.

input: A shared deck contains hundreds of generic words unrelated to the learner's current material.
expected: Does not import the shared deck wholesale merely because it is available.
May mine useful entries as candidates.
Requires the same usefulness/context/review-cost test as learner-supplied material.

input: An absolute beginner has almost no comprehensible personal material yet, but a well-structured frequency deck with clear target forms, meanings and trustworthy audio is available.
expected: May use the frequency/shared deck as a bootstrap candidate source.
Inspects fields, information density, script/readings and audio quality before selecting items.
Does not import the entire deck blindly into the workflow.
Selects only useful items and shifts toward personally encountered contextual material as the learner progresses.

input: A YouTube setup guide says to use 50 new cards/day, 9999 maximum reviews, one 10-minute learning step and a fixed display-order preset.
expected: Does not copy the numeric preset as a universal workflow recommendation.
Uses current official Anki/FSRS documentation as the source of truth.
Relates desired retention/new-card intake to the learner's sustainable review workload and review history.
Treats learning steps and display order as version-sensitive settings rather than permanent card-generation rules.

input: A guide claims that Descending retrievability prioritizes the cards most at risk of being forgotten under FSRS.
expected: Rejects that claim under current Anki semantics.
Uses Ascending retrievability when the goal is to prioritize lower-retrievability cards in a large backlog.
Prefers Due date, then random when the learner is up to date or has only a small backlog.

input: The same source sentence produces separate Reading and Production cards in the current workflow. The user asks whether enabling Anki sibling burying will automatically keep them apart.
expected: Explains that the current builder creates one note per planned card.
Does not claim that those cross-skill cards are Anki siblings.
Explains that native sibling burying only affects multiple cards generated from the same note.

input: A candidate sentence contains the useful target expression plus three other unfamiliar words. Another natural sentence contains the same target and all surrounding words are already understood.
expected: Prefers the cleaner near-i+1 sentence.
Keeps one primary unknown/focus item.
Does not force the denser sentence merely because it came from the original source.
If no clean sentence exists, may split targets, seek another context, or skip.

input: A target word has a literal sense, a common figurative sense, and several example sentences available.
expected: Inspects multiple trustworthy contexts before deciding which senses matter.
Does not paste six or more example sentences onto the review front.
Uses one clear primary context per card.
Creates separate sense cards only when the senses are distinct and independently useful; otherwise keeps extra examples concise and secondary.

input: An AI-generated sentence is grammatical but its naturalness/register is uncertain. A native-source sentence expresses the same useful chunk naturally.
expected: Prefers the attested/native sentence for an exact Production target.
Does not train the uncertain AI sentence verbatim without sufficient validation.
May use a direct semantic production prompt when no trustworthy full sentence is available.
Keeps generated passive-support examples subject to correctness/naturalness checks as well.

input: A Production card has answer audio, but pronunciation/prosody is not a meaningful difficulty for this item.
expected: Does not create an extra Pronunciation card solely because shadowing is possible.
Does not make repeated shadowing mandatory for every review.
May suggest brief post-answer shadowing only when pronunciation/prosody has real learning value.

input: A dictionary lists five different glosses for one target word, but the source sentence clearly uses only one common sense.
expected: Uses the source/context to identify the primary sense being learned.
Does not require recalling all five dictionary glosses from one card.
Creates another card only if another sense is distinct, useful, and independently worth reviewing.

input: AI proposes that a target word is cognate with a familiar word, but no trustworthy etymological support has been checked. A sound-alike mnemonic is still possible.
expected: Does not present the proposed cognate/etymology as fact without verification.
May use the sound-alike association if helpful, but labels it as a mnemonic rather than etymology.
Skips the mnemonic entirely if it adds more complexity than memory benefit.

input: The learner correctly recalls a word after four seconds with noticeable hesitation. A creator's rule says anything over two seconds must be Again.
expected: Rejects the fixed two-second failure rule.
Treats correct but slow/doubtful recall as compatible with Hard under current Anki semantics.
Uses Again only when the answer is incorrect or could not be recalled.

input: The user sets Anki's on-screen timer to three seconds and asks whether the card now automatically fails or changes its interval after three seconds.
expected: Explains that the normal on-screen/internal timer does not influence scheduling by itself.
Explains that Maximum answer seconds caps recorded timing statistics rather than failing the card.
Mentions Auto Advance only if the user actually wants automatic timed actions.

input: A useful mature language deck still contains valuable scheduled reviews, but a creator recommends abandoning every deck after one month to save time.
expected: Does not recommend fixed monthly retirement of worthwhile mature cards.
Controls workload by reducing new cards, pruning redundancy, and fixing/suspending low-value leeches instead.
Preserves long-term spaced reviews for cards that still justify their review cost.

input: The learner repeatedly confuses two target-language prepositions. The useful knowledge is the distinction between them in one specific context.
expected: May create one contrast/discrimination card because the relationship itself is the primary retrieval target.
Keeps the prompt constrained to one decision/contrast.
Does not turn the card into a mega-card asking for several unrelated translations, rules, and examples.

input: The learner can answer one familiar sentence instantly after many reviews but fails to recognize/use the same target chunk in a new natural context.
expected: Does not treat speed on the familiar card as sufficient evidence of flexible mastery.
Identifies possible cue overfitting to the card wording.
If another card is genuinely useful, varies the natural context or retrieval direction rather than cloning the original wording.
Does not create extra variants solely to increase volume.

input: An existing isolated vocabulary scaffold has strong review-history mastery and a richer contextual card now fully covers the same recognition target. The user is maintaining the collection.
expected: May recommend retiring or suspending the redundant scaffold to reduce future review cost.
Requires reliable mastery evidence and verifies that no distinct skill gap is lost.
Does not infer mastery from card age alone.
Does not delete the user's existing card without permission.

input: A valuable card repeatedly fails because the learner confuses two near-synonyms despite repeated exposure to the same isolated definition.
expected: Diagnoses the confusion instead of creating duplicate copies for brute-force repetition.
May replace or supplement the prompt with a concise contextual contrast that distinguishes the near-synonyms.
Keeps one primary retrieval decision and avoids turning the back into a long lesson.
Removes/suspends the card only if it is low-value or remains unsuitable after repair.

input: The learner is reading a comprehensible short story with several unknown words but can still follow the plot.
expected: Prefers a meaning-first pass instead of interrupting the story to look up every unknown word.
Preserves/marks useful context and evaluates unknown items after the passage or on a later pass.
Uses lookup selectively based on usefulness and whether the unknown actually blocks comprehension.
Does not require a second pass when the source is already isolated/short or another workflow is clearly more efficient.

input: A learner repeatedly confuses the grammatical gender of a useful noun. The real target phrase contains the correct determiner, and a stable visual/action mnemonic could help.
expected: Keeps the real linguistic form such as determiner + noun as the primary knowledge to retrieve.
May add a stable concrete mnemonic code as secondary scaffolding.
Uses the same mapping consistently within the language/deck.
Does not create an extra card solely for the mnemonic.
Does not hard-code a universal mapping such as sparkling=feminine for every learner.

input: A useful abstract expression is clear with a concise base-language cue; the video method would otherwise add an image and automatic forward/reverse cards.
expected: Does not search for an ambiguous/decorative image merely because the source method recommends images.
Does not create automatic reverse cards.
Uses the configured base language when it gives the clearest efficient cue.
Creates extra retrieval directions only when they independently justify future review cost.

input: A Chinese vocabulary item has target text, pinyin, a simplified variant, and a concise grammatical label. Only written recognition is currently worth training.
expected: Keeps the selected Reading card as the only card unless another skill independently adds value.
Stores pinyin/reading aid in the structured reading field.
Stores the alternate written form in variant.
Stores the concise grammatical label in grammar.
Does not create Listening, Production, or Pronunciation cards merely because those fields are populated.

input: A card tests the meaning of a written target item; decoding/pronunciation is not being tested and a reading aid would remove irrelevant difficulty.
expected: May show the reading/pronunciation aid as support because it is not the retrieval target.
Keeps the target meaning hidden until answer reveal.
If the card instead tests script decoding/pronunciation, hides the reading aid because it would become the answer.

input: The learner studies Chinese characters and actively wants to practice writing a subset from memory.
expected: May create a Production card whose task is active written/handwriting recall.
Does not add a new handwriting deck or card type family.
Creates handwriting cards only for items where active written output is independently useful.

input: One source item has reading, variant, grammar, audio, and image fields, but only one retrieval skill is worth reviewing.
expected: Uses the rich structured data without turning every field into a card.
Keeps the current one-note-per-selected-planned-card workflow behavior.
Does not auto-generate reverse or sibling cards simply because Anki technically supports multiple templates.

input: During immersion, the learner finds a potentially useful word but its intended sense/register is still unclear. The card could be created immediately and 'figured out' through future failed reviews.
expected: Keeps the item as a candidate until the intended meaning/form/usage is clarified enough to encode.
Does not rely on repeated Anki failures to perform first-time semantic discovery.
Does not require prior mastery; clarification may happen immediately before card creation.
May still use vetted beginner bootstrap material when its target meaning/form is sufficiently clear.

input: The learner wants a simple pass/fail review workflow because four answer buttons create decision friction.
expected: Explains that current Anki can be used natively with only Again for incorrect answers and Good for correct answers.
Does not require a Pass/Fail add-on merely to obtain binary grading.
Does not claim Hard or Easy inherently break FSRS or the scheduler.
Keeps Again for forgotten/incorrect answers rather than using Hard as a failure grade.

input: The learner returns to a useful language deck after several weeks away and has a large review backlog.
expected: Does not recommend deleting or resetting the useful deck solely because reviews accumulated.
Explains that Anki can resume after a long break and accounts for overdue delay in subsequent scheduling.
May reduce or pause new cards while the backlog is handled at a sustainable pace.
Prunes/suspends cards only for evidence-based low value, redundancy, or card-quality problems rather than a fixed age threshold.

input: A useful Norwegian noun has a non-obvious grammatical gender and an irregular plural. The learner repeatedly needs both in active speech, while the base meaning is already easy.
expected: May create separate atomic Production retrievals for the determiner+noun gender form and the irregular plural because each is independently useful.
Keeps one primary feature/form per card instead of asking for gender, singular, plural, translation, and explanation all at once.
May reveal already-known meaning/context when that isolates the grammatical form being tested.
Keeps the cards in the existing skill decks and uses grammar/word-form metadata or tags instead of creating a Norwegian-specific microdeck or note model.

input: A source note contains an entire verb paradigm, but only the irregular past form is currently difficult and useful for the learner.
expected: Targets the irregular past form if it independently deserves review.
Does not create cards for every tense/person merely because the paradigm is available.
Uses a constrained lemma/context/function cue so the learner knows which form to retrieve.
Skips predictable or already-automatic forms that do not justify future review cost.

input: A useful Japanese sentence was mined from a video at 07:14. The card already has the sentence, meaning, and useful audio.
expected: Keeps the exact video timestamp or equivalent stable locator in the source/provenance field when available.
Does not create an extra card just for the timestamp.
Does not invent a more precise timestamp or locator than the source provides.
Uses the locator to make the original context easy to reopen if the card later needs verification or repair.

input: An existing workflow-created language deck has several cards with repeated Again reviews. The user asks the AI to analyze why they are difficult and improve the collection.
expected: Starts by inspecting card fields/source context and review history without mutating the collection.
Treats repeated Again reviews as evidence that a card deserves inspection, not as proof of one specific cause.
Diagnoses possibilities such as ambiguity, insufficient context, confusable items, missing prerequisite, malformed content, genuine difficulty, or low value.
Proposes the smallest justified repair.
Requires explicit user approval before rewriting, suspending, deleting, rescheduling, or reprioritizing existing cards.

input: The learner started from a vetted frequency deck but can now comfortably understand useful native content. The generic deck still has hundreds of unseen items, while personally encountered sentences are available.
expected: Does not keep prioritizing the generic frequency source merely because unseen cards remain.
Prefers personally encountered/context-rich candidates when they are useful and comprehensible enough.
Treats the source transition as evidence-driven rather than requiring a fixed Refold phase or vocabulary-count milestone.
May still use shared/frequency material selectively when it fills a real gap.

input: During repeated speaking practice, the learner keeps failing to express one useful idea. They provide the base-language thought but no verified target-language wording.
expected: Treats the real output failure as a candidate source because it reflects an actual useful gap.
Does not convert the base-language thought directly into an unverified literal Production answer.
Finds or verifies a natural target-language expression for the intended meaning, variety, and register before scheduling Production.
Creates a card only if the gap is useful enough to justify future review cost and preserves attested context/source when possible.

input: A textbook section states a grammar rule, gives a full conjugation table, and provides contextual examples. The learner mainly needs to choose the correct form in ordinary sentences, not recite the wording of the rule.
expected: Does not automatically create a declarative rule-recall card merely because the rule is written in the source.
Identifies contextual application/production as the useful retrieval target.
Uses constrained Production or an unambiguous cloze/contextual task rather than a full-table recall card.
Keeps one primary grammatical decision/form per card and avoids dumping the complete paradigm onto one card.
May add a brief back-side explanation of the rule only when it helps verify or prevent confusion.

input: The learner encounters a useful domain-specific target-language term that matters for their work but appears only rarely in normal input. Another unknown term is equally rare but obscure, low-value, and unrelated to the learner's goals.
expected: Treats low natural re-encounter frequency as a positive SRS signal only when the item is genuinely useful.
May create a card for the useful domain-specific term because natural exposure is unlikely to reinforce it soon.
Skips the obscure low-value term even though it is also rare.
Does not use a fixed corpus-frequency cutoff or vocabulary-count threshold.
Still requires clarity/context and future review cost to justify the card.

input: Six separate French dialogue lines were used to create six Pronunciation cards. Their fronts all say only 'Say this naturally in French, then compare with the recording' with no visible phrase and no front audio; their full written target is revealed only on the back.
expected: Rejects the six indistinguishable unanswerable fronts instead of keeping them as-is.
For genuine read-aloud practice, uses the written target as the front cue and answer audio on the back.
For audio identification, puts sound on the front without leaking the written target.
Does not create Pronunciation for every dialogue line by default; requires distinct useful pronunciation difficulty.

input: A useful dialogue line contains the expression 'depuis l’âge de'. A proposed Production card demands an exact long French sentence corresponding to a broad base-language cue, even though several natural French sentences could answer the cue.
expected: Identifies whether the important retrieval target is the reusable construction rather than the entire sentence.
Prefers a concise contextual Production card for the phrase when that is the actual learning goal.
Only requires entire exact wording when that wording is itself the target and clearly constrained.
Accepts natural alternate correct French formulations instead of treating the stored full example as the only possible answer.

input: A single audio clip taken from a long dialogue utterance is reused for Listening, Production, and Pronunciation cards. Those cards contain different target-language strings and the recording's verified transcript is missing.
expected: Does not infer that identical audio bytes prove alignment with all different target texts.
Obtains/verifies the actual clip transcript or creates separate focused clips instead of silently reusing audio.
Provides audio_transcript consistently for all distinct target uses when one recording is intentionally shared.
Avoids presenting a different/longer utterance as the exact pronunciation of a target that it does not contain.
Retains the user-selected base language rather than changing English to Portuguese without consent.

input: Learner sends screenshots containing only long, multi-clause French sentences (no short isolated phrases) and asks for rapid, efficient Anki cards. One line says: 'Vous pouvez me suivre, c'est à deux minutes d'ici.'
expected: Understands each complete line, then actively mines natural, useful shorter chunks even though all supplied sentences are long.
May select 'vous pouvez me suivre' and 'à deux minutes d'ici' as separate candidates when each is useful and unknown, with separate concise retrieval prompts.
Does not create a full-sentence card merely because the input line is long, nor force the learner to reproduce both clauses at once.
May generate zero, one, or several cards from that line based on distinct usefulness; never one card per clause by default.
Preserves the source locator and avoids wasting review time with unrelated full-sentence front context.

input: Learner supplies a lengthy sentence containing the idiom 'avoir beau essayer' and other familiar text. Simple cutting by commas or words would break the idiom into nonsensical fragments.
expected: Preserves the idiom/verb construction as one meaningful learning unit, with the context needed to distinguish the intended sense.
Does not cut inside an idiom or make standalone cards for semantically empty fragments.
Selects only genuinely useful chunks from the surrounding long sentence; may skip the rest.
Makes the resulting card quick to understand, retrieve and verify.

input: A long source sentence is also a genuinely useful complete routine utterance whose overall conversational function is the learner's intended target. Other sentences from the same source are long but contain one short new collocation each.
expected: Retains the complete utterance only if reproducing/recognizing the whole is independently valuable and review remains quick.
Prefers short, natural chunks for the other lines, not exact memorization of full multi-clause text.
Does not enforce a fixed word limit, chunk quota, or requirement that every sentence yield a card.
Uses clear single-target fronts and quick-to-check backs; omits ambiguous or high-effort candidates.

input: A long French audio dialogue and full transcript contain several short useful expressions. The learner wants quick Listening cards for only two expressions, without replaying the entire audio or making cards for every clause.
expected: Selects only the useful independent expressions, not the whole recording as the target of each card.
Uses the matching audio_clip for each selected spoken chunk with source-verified timestamps or conservative alignment, never a full-dialogue audio attachment.
Preserves the exact meaning, natural context, and source locator, and blocks ambiguous audio cuts for clarification.
Does not create additional full-line Listening/Pronunciation cards unless they train an independently valuable skill.
